I want to start off by saying thank you to Voat for allowing me to even feel brave enough to post something that on many platforms could be construed as controversial. I hope the discussions can continue.

I'm sure most people can agree the US tax code is a mess, full of inconsistencies and nonsense. And while I personally am against taxes, I am reasonable enough to understand they are not going away any time soon. I am honestly curious if Voat believes the FairTax is a viable alternative. Why or why not? It seems to be pretty reasonable. It accounts for the impoverished and proportionally taxes those who consume more (some would say the wealthy fit into this category). So what's the deal? Info for those curious.
Does Voat like the FairTax? (serious) Why do you or don't you support it?
I'm for it. It's so much less conveluted.

On the one hand, it works, more or less, in Texas. At least, when I lived there. There wasn't an income tax, but sales tax was something like 12%. (If you actually live in Texas and my numbers aren't quite right, I apologize. It's been a long time since I lived there.)

On the other hand, it would raise the apparent price of almost everything, which would create a reduction in spending. At least for awhile until the higher prices became the new norm.

It'd certainly make tax evasion easier. I know I'd shop more with local farmers, who definitely aren't charging sales tax, rather than go to the grocery store. Craig's List would probably see an uptick in use as well.

Theory aside, though, it'll never happen. There isn't a single Democrat in Washington that will vote for a tax plan that eliminates capital gains taxes.
I agree with you that the apparent cost of goods would increase, but wouldn't your paycheck also be larger (plus the value added from the prebate) since most income taxes are eliminated?
Oh, absolutely. But people will see the higher prices and back off spending. At least for awhile. And that's not a "People are stoopid" remark- it's just the way our brains work.

I don't like it because while it is simple, it shifts the tax burden to the poor because proportionally much more of poor people's income is spent on consumption. http://www.forbes.com/sites/beltway/2015/05/27/the-trouble-with-the-fairtax/ For the record, I would benefit from it.

My understanding had the prebate sent to each individual addressing this issue effectively taxing purchases above a certain amount spent. I believe it scales with inflation and number of adults and children in the household. A flat tax would disproportionately affect the poor since 14% of $1 is felt more than 14% of $10000.
I am opposed mostly because it could only ever work if it were set up as a VAT. It also does not address the fact that .1% of the population control >80% of the money

I'm confused. The FairTax would eliminate the VAT since business are not taxed on raw goods and labor. The 0.1% buy things, too. Reinvesting in business is also good for the economy because the result is usually more jobs or better products.

This is my boo the government rant, but the 0.1% make their money from stocks which are currently artificially overvalued thanks to the FED's QE programs. They could "theoretically" lose that money if the market fell (assuming they don't have someone saying uhh pull out now the market is going to fall tomorrow). Crony business/government relationships are a bitch.

I'm saying a 20+% tax levied at the point of sale would likely be circumvented on a large scale, a VAT spreads that tax out over the production life of a product making it easier to collect more of the tax. Certainly the top earners spend more but not as much more as they earn, almost by definition. I see no problem with someone who makes multiple millions per year paying a greater than 50% income tax, but having 5 tax brackets that all trigger at less than 200k is retarded given the distribution of wealth and current dollar value of goods.

I have seen the argument that the pos would be circumvented, but that is conjecture and there is no way to truly test if that is true (is it really worth all the hassle to buy milk from another country?). There are also so many more reasons why the price of goods could go down once the cost of manufacturing goods is theoretically lowered thus negating the idea people would want to circumvent the tax in the first place since goods would be only modestly more expensive.

A VAT tax is already in place and has made goods more expensive for the consumers only since the cost is simply passed down the chain to the final purchasing price. This is a double tax for those paying into the system since you are not only taxed on your income but also paying the taxes for companies who have passed their cost down to you.

Rich people don't usually pay income tax and find ways around the current tax code. It is more of a burden to avoid a consumption tax on most items than it is to just pay what could arguably be no more than a few percentage points difference in price.

I am not an economist, so my views may be skewed/flawed. If they are, I would welcome a patient, down to earth explanation of the issue.

My issue is that this method of taxation requires you to purchase something. There are plenty of problems with this model, however the one that stands out the furthest in my eyes is that the people who control the most wealth don't actually purchase many goods. They put the money back into investments and gain more wealth. The lower rungs of society must kick back out the majority of their earnings to support themselves. This would create a taxation scenario that unfairly favors the wealthiest members of society.

I will address your point about the rich, but let me make one point. To me this model does favors those who save, but you do have to buy basic necessities to live. To be completely honest, if someone thinks they beat the system by living only on the amount covered by the rebate good on them. I wish I was not as materialistic.

Your issue with investments. This might have changed since the crony relationship between the government and business seems to be getting stronger every day, but I'll take a stab at it. An investment is supposed to be used to support and grow a company which produces a product that is in demand. If a rich person makes his money by investing in a business which then hires people to in turn make a good, I'm ok if the investor makes more money. They should. They are putting up a big risk. They could easily lose it all (I know this can be debated) with one bad investment.

Thoughts?

Agreed on the investments. I was unclear why I brought that up, it was more of a way to say how the wealthy have money, but it is tied up elsewhere, not being actively spent or taxed. If the flat tax was applied to investments as well, I would support that aspect more.

This next point, I have to establish that I think an option to opt out of a governmental group should exist, that option would have them stop paying tax, but would also stop any protective/productive measures that governmental body provides as well. No tax = most freedom but also = no school, no military/police defense (someone could kidnap you and you alone are the person responsible to get you out of that position), no usage of government maintained roads, etc. This would effectively be individual anarchism.

I don't like the idea of someone beating the tax system at all. If there is a governmental body providing a structure, benefits, protections, abilities to an individual, that individual is benefiting. If they game out a way to benefit without paying taxes or in some other manner contributing back to the system, they are effectively stealing from those who are investing in the government.

So I would say not good on them if they lived within that rebate, they are screwing over the others around them, and shuffling off their responsibilities to others, greed incarnate.

The current capital gains tax is essentially a flat tax and pretty close to the FairTax number (I believe 12 or 15% if someone wants to fact check). But I don't think someone taking such a big risk to create or support a new business should have to be punished for doing so, do you? If so that's fine but I can tell you as a very small p2p investor myself, I would be pissed if I was taking such a huge risk lending to someone at 12% and then paying 35% tax on the earnings. That's just not worth the risk. I would put my money somewhere that would arguably be less productive.

Your idea makes sense to me. Run for office ;)

The number of people who chose to live like that are probably going to be so few they were not really contributing to society any way. I just think of it as a very very minor write off. They probably don't go outside or anything lol.

The biggest issue is that the idea for government based protection starts pushing into scifi. You would need a govt based forcefield to protect you from the anarchists, then there is the whole issue with corruption there too.

Ultimately, everything would be easy in a perfect world. But what we have now is like the first Witcher videogame, choose the least of evils and hope for the best.

Having said all this I have a plan to make evesdropping on telephone conversations very difficult to understand by the person(s) intercepting it.

Microprocessors are cheap. There would be 2 or more devices with the same key that the microprocessor would invert and vary the conversation amplitude and frequency according to the same random number set on both devices. These would be independent of the telephones and 'encrypt' the audio before it gets to the phone and after it leaves the phone. It would sound like the old modem and fax telephone signals because it could be acoustically coupled to and from the phone.
